issues.legal_issue: A will may be admitted to probate when its valid execution and the testator’s testamentary capacity are established, the challenger does not prove fraud, coercion or undue influence, and any suspicious circumstances are satisfactorily explained.
material_facts: The will left the testator’s entire estate to his second wife and made no provision for his mother or youngest daughter, circumstances the challengers relied on as suspicious and unnatural.
The courts accepted evidence that the testator signed the will in the presence of two witnesses, who attested it in his presence and in each other’s presence.
There was no effective challenge to the testator’s testamentary capacity and no evidence that he lacked a sound disposing mind or failed to understand the will’s effect.
The courts found that the second wife was present but had no part in preparing or executing the will.

The testator’s relations with his son and two daughters were hostile; he had already made arrangements for his daughters’ maintenance and considered that he could provide for his mother and youngest daughter during his lifetime.
The evidence accepted by the courts showed that the will was executed and attested on the same occasion and that the alleged later addition of the attestation clause was not established.
issues.conclusion: The will was genuine, validly executed and duly attested by a testator in a sound disposing state of mind; the grant of probate was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The propounder must establish the testator’s signature, sound disposing mind, understanding of the nature and effect of the dispositions, free volition, and execution in the presence of two attesting witnesses who attest in the testator’s presence and in each other’s presence. Once established, that burden is discharged, but legitimate suspicious circumstances must be satisfactorily explained by the propounder. If the propounder takes a prominent part in execution and receives a substantial benefit, that is itself suspicious. The challenger bears the burden of proving allegations of fraud, coercion or undue influence. A testator’s choice is not displaced merely because it appears foolish or heartless if made with full comprehension. These principles were drawn from H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B. N. Thimmajamma, Rani Purnima Devi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Dev, and Motibai Hormusjee Kanga v. Jamsetjee Hormusjee Kanga.

rule.if: probate_proceeding and valid_execution_and_attestation_proved and testamentary_capacity_and_understanding_proved and (suspicious_circumstances_satisfactorily_explained or no_legitimate_suspicious_circumstances_remain) and challenger_fails_to_prove_fraud_coercion_or_undue_influence

predicates.probate_proceeding: The dispute concerns whether a will should be admitted to probate.
predicates.valid_execution_and_attestation_proved: The propounder establishes that the testator signed the will and that the required witnesses attested it in the testator’s presence and in each other’s presence.
predicates.testamentary_capacity_and_understanding_: The evidence establishes that the testator had a sound disposing mind and understood the nature and effect of the will’s dispositions.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_satisfactorily_: The propounder gives a satisfactory explanation for legitimate circumstances surrounding the will that could cast doubt on its genuineness or free execution.
predicates.no_legitimate_suspicious_circumstances_r: The evidence does not leave any legitimate circumstance that reasonably casts doubt on the will’s genuineness or the testator’s free will and mind.
predicates.challenger_fails_to_prove_fraud_coercion: The person challenging the will does not establish that it was procured by fraud, coercion or undue influence.

issues.definition: When a probate proceeding establishes valid execution and testamentary capacity, and no unexplained legitimate suspicion or proved fraud, coercion or undue influence remains, probate must be granted.

issues.legal_issue: A presumption of undue influence does not arise merely from a relationship between a testator and a person to whom the testator is engaged or married, and a foreign presumption cannot be applied without regard to local conditions and the governing rules of evidence.
material_facts: The will benefited the testator’s newly married wife, who had been engaged to him shortly before the marriage and was present when he executed it.
The wife’s mother had initiated the correspondence on her behalf, and the evidence showed that companionship was the parties’ principal consideration in arranging the marriage.
The courts found no evidence that the wife dominated the testator’s will, imposed the will as a condition of marriage, or took part in its execution.
The will was executed after the marriage; the evidence accepted by the courts did not establish that it was executed before the marriage.
The challengers relied on an English legal text describing a presumption of undue influence in a relationship between an engaged man and woman.
issues.conclusion: The relationship did not give rise to a presumption of undue influence; the challenger had to prove undue influence, and the evidence did not do so.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 103, 111 and 114 of the Indian Evidence Act, the burden of substantiating a special plea of undue influence rests on the party who raises it; the relationship in this case did not fall within section 111, and any inference under section 114 must be justified by facts making it reasonable and natural. A presumption drawn from foreign law should not be transplanted without critical consideration of its principles and their applicability to local social conditions. A foreign decision may assist where an objective principle arises from pari materia legislation and is applicable to local conditions.

predicates.probate_proceeding: The dispute concerns whether a will should be admitted to probate.
predicates.undue_influence_alleged: A person challenging the will alleges that it was procured through undue influence.
predicates.relationship_is_the_basis_for_presumed_d: The alleged basis for presuming undue influence is the testator’s relationship with the beneficiary, such as engagement or marriage.
predicates.no_independent_evidence_proves_undue_inf: The evidence does not independently establish that the beneficiary overbore the testator’s free will or procured the disposition through undue influence.

issues.definition: In a probate proceeding, when undue influence is alleged on the basis of the testator’s relationship with a beneficiary and no independent evidence proves it, the challenger must prove undue influence and it is not presumed from that relationship.
